title: Deb's Wayfinding Talk
speaker: Manja Deb Wibe
summary: Manja Deb Wibe shares that their life journey has been shaped by various influences, but ultimately came to understand that true meaning and liberation lie not in trying to control or perfect their experiences, but rather in embracing the present moment as it is. This realization has brought a sense of freedom from ego and perfectionism, allowing them to find peace and fulfillment in being fully engaged with life. Through regular meditation practice, they've discovered a deeper connection to themselves and others, finding a sense of home and transformation that transcends external circumstances.

sentences.text: I'm not quite, as you can tell, not used to the [unclear: "formalist"].
I can follow, but I don't lead well.
Whoops, and there it goes.
So again, good evening.
Thank you for being here.
I'm very glad to be here with you.
It's been a long time.
I've been away with my daughter, who had a new baby, and I've been having a delightful time being a grandma for the third time around.
Then my family came from the prairies to visit us and to see the new baby, who's in Vancouver, BC.
They gave me the invite to join them for a tour down the coast.
So that has meant a lengthy time away.
It was wonderful, and I'm just very happy to be back here with you all tonight.
I was visiting with Tim some time ago in [unclear: "Daksang"].
I don't remember exactly how the conversation was going, but I think I asked him something about becoming more deeply immersed in practice here at Red Cedar.
He said, "Aha, maybe this is the time for a wayfinding talk."
I didn't know what a wayfinding talk was, but I figured it out because I heard some other folks talking.
I figured wayfinding probably meant finding your way to practice.
So that's what this talk is all about.
It's my wayfinding talk.
When Tim mentioned that, it sounded easy enough.
In fact, all of us know our own history, so how hard can it be?
But I found it amazingly challenging.
Every life is like a multifaceted crystal.
You turn it one way and you see one color.
You turn it another way and get a different color.
Each color is like a storyline in our lives.
So there are literally thousands of storylines, even for a single thing like wayfinding.
When we're born, none of us is aware that we're already endowed with genetic makeup that will tend to lend to us a perspective, maybe a very particular perspective.
None of us is aware that the family we're born into or the culture that surrounds us will have such a huge impact on how we view the world and how we experience it.
So over time, we come to believe that the sum of these influences and the experiences are who we are.
I was born a Taurus in the middle of the North Dakota prairie, for those of you who are believers in stars or the influence of stars and planets.
My folks were longtime prairie people, small town folks who were tied to the land, the church, and the community.
They believed in hard work and strict upbringing, but they also believed in having fun.
There wasn't a lot to do in the very small town in which I was raised, so we relied on our imagination, and with two sisters and a brother and a lot of friends around, we became quite imaginative.
I was a shy kid, a serious kid, a bit too serious I'm afraid.
I remember lying awake at night feeling like I had the weight of the world on my shoulders.
I mean literally, literally.
For some strange reason, unbeknownst to me yet, I'd picked up the idea that the well-being of the world relied on the regularity of my prayers.
I don't know where that idea came from, but maybe from the same place that the idea that I had to be perfect came from.
Perfection became, or perfectionism became, a deep running theme in my life, and because I was hardly perfect, so did the idea that I wasn't good enough.
So I spent a lot of time and effort trying to be.
That's a big challenge, and it's awfully exhausting, and I wasn't too good at it.
As I grew older, I became driven by the idea that if I could only understand the world, then I could do what I'm supposed to do, and everything would be all right.
Of course, I didn't realize that this was what was driving me back in those days.
An inner restlessness kept me running from one thing to another thing, trying to reach something that I didn't even know existed.
I married just out of nursing school.
I had three beautiful kids, and then I divorced when I didn't find what I was looking for.
This was followed by years of searching through various relationships, various paths of spirituality, careers, and geographical locations.
I can't count the number of moves on my two fingers.

In 1989, I entered a graduate program in philosophy at the University of Kansas, thinking that all of these great minds must know something I don't, and that what they knew might be able to end this deep hunger, this deep quest, that had been driving me all these years.
Not surprisingly, they offered more questions than answers.

But graduate school was an education for an early middle-aged prairie girl, and the experience, actually more than the book learning, offered me a whole new, though no less perplexing, perspective of the world.
Being a single mom, working as a nurse and as a teaching assistant, and going to graduate school was no small feat.
I was nearly empty, certainly very close, when I met Stan Lombardo on the steps of the cafeteria one day.
I can't remember how our conversation started, but I found out that Stan was the guiding teacher for the Southwind Zen Center in Lawrence, Kansas.
I had some exposure to Eastern thinking, both due to my own studies and due to my graduate studies, and I was very interested in exploring practice.
But I had a son who was going through a really difficult time, and I just couldn't even imagine how I might balance early morning practices and long retreats.
But Stan had an answer, as he typically seemed to do.
He said that he had a son my son's own age, and that it would be just great if the boys hung out.
So one morning I found myself sitting on a cushion, and my life began to change in small ways at first.
Not so small that my kids didn't notice.

A friend of mine had given me the name Whirling Dervish because I was always whirling off at something, some good deed, social activism, whatever it was, or whirling in whatever activity happened to be available.
I think he didn't name me Whirling Dervish, obviously, after a Sufi, but more like a Tasmanian devil.
And so, sorry, I'm working on this thing.
It hadn't passed the notice of my kids, my practicing.
When I was having a particularly wildly whirling day, I remember my daughter Anna saying to me, "Mom, you need to go back to practice.
You're really different when you've been sitting."
So I sat, and eventually I took the precepts.
One retreat followed another, and eventually, the summer after my daughter graduated from high school, I moved into the Zen Center.
Zen Master [unclear: "Sung Song"], the head of the Korean [unclear: "Quantum"] School of Zen and the head of our school, always said that it was good to live at a Zen Center.
He said living together is like putting field potatoes in a potato washer.
I don't know if any of you remember those kinds of things.
He said rubbing up against one another tends to get the dirt off.
In this case, what he meant is it helps us to see our own minds and to drop our ideas about how things ought to be.
He was right.
Living at the Zen Center, access to regular practice with a sangha, daily sitting, long hours on retreat, forced me to begin to see my own mind.
It began the journey of understanding something I'd never gotten before, and that's that I am not my thoughts.
Who I think I am is only a compilation of my experiences and the perspectives that arise from them.
And who I truly am, in fact, whatever I am, I am, and who I truly am, in fact, whatever truly is, lies before thinking, discoverable only in the moment, this very moment.
How amazingly liberating.
However, it was going to take a lot more life and a lot more practice before that idea really became transformed into a living reality that I could trust.
I eventually ended up leaving the Zen Center and moving back to North Dakota in order to be with my youngest son as he completed his final year of high school.
It was difficult to leave my sangha.
My guiding teacher encouraged me to become a dharma teacher.
Imagine that.
And he asked me to begin offering sitting practice in the town where I settled.
It was quite an oddity for the community.

A few curiosity seekers actually showed up at the door, managed to sit on the cushions, lovely folks, but after two attempts to start the group, and some pretty unusual feedback from my community, I finally let it go.
For the next 13 years, I ended up sitting solo in the upstairs room of my old farmhouse.
Then one day, I realized that that wasn't enough.
Funny it took me so long.
I felt hungry.
It had been a growing hunger for a long, long time, but it couldn't be ignored anymore.
I knew that I needed to reconnect.
I needed sangha.
So I checked out the possibilities of practice in the Bellingham area.
My oldest son had lived in Bellingham for a period of time, and I had visited him often and had fallen in love with it.
So I thought, why not?
I packed up my bags and moved out, and eventually found you, of which I'm really grateful.
I wanted to have a deeper, more inspiring story for you tonight, a teaching story.
But what I have for you is my wayfinding story, or at least a facet of it.
What this wayfinding story doesn't tell you or clearly convey is the incredible gratitude that I have for this practice, and the incredible, profound power of this practice.
It's taught me how to let go of striving and to just be in the moment.
It's brought a woman crippled by perfectionism into a new life.
Learning that there is nowhere to go, nothing to do, and nothing to search for has brought me home to this moment, to this breath.
And in that is the power to transform a whirling dervish and so much more.
I'm not perfect.
What this practice has taught me is that I don't have to be.
My daughter has a poster in her living room.
She's carried it with her for years.
It carries a quote from Thich Nhat Hanh.
It says:
*I have arrived.
I am home.
My destination is in each step.*
This practice has brought me home.
And it's made all the difference.
